newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N.-U.S. approves supplies for Iraq faster.
newsitem.headline: U.N.-U.S. approves supplies for Iraq faster.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday lifted its objections to 13 contracts for goods to Iraq under a humanitarian plan allowing Baghdad to sell some of its oil despite trade sanctions, diplomats said.

The contracts were for soap and detergent, which Washington had delayed in the Security Council's sanctions committee because of concerns there were not enough U.N. monitors in Iraq to supervise proper distribution.

At issue is a so-called oil-for-food plan allowing Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to purchase necessities for its people under sanctions since Baghdad invaded Kuwait in August 1990. The plan went into effect on Dec. 10 but no goods have reached Iraq yet.
"It was important that the observers be in place in Iraq to ensure that the materials would reach the Iraqi people," a U.S. official said.

He said that key Security Council members had been assured by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan that enough observers were now in Baghdad. U.N. sources said earlier that getting staff and transport to Iraq quickly had been a problem.

In addition to the soap, the sanctions committee also allowed another four contracts for food and medicine to be shipped to Baghdad. A total of 32 contracts for goods have now been approved, more than half of them on Wednesday.

Iraq has complained bitterly about both the United Nations secretariat and the sanctions committee. It said contracts had been signed with more than 280 suppliers but that U.N. procedures and politics prevented food, medicine and other necessities from reaching the country.

Part of the delays were attributed to stringent procedures set up by the Security Council to make sure the goods shipped to Iraq fall under its guidelines. In addition the United Nations had to make sure there was enough money deposited in a special escrow account from oil sales to pay suppliers.
Other delays have resulted from ships used by the suppliers taking weeks to arrive, U.N. officials said.

Annan, in a report to the Security Council on Tuesday, said the oil contracts, amounting to more than $1 billion so far, were expedited quickly but the food and other supplies proved far more complicated. He said he did not expect all the goods to be delivered within a six-month period.
The United Nations is fielding some 151 monitors to make sure Iraqi authorities distribute goods equitably and to help evaluate the country's needs.
